reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Cardinal feature is excessive daytime sleepiness with irresistible sleep attacks, often accompanied by a classic tetrad that also includes cataplexy, sleep paralysis, and hypnagogic hallucinations
Cataplexy, sudden transient loss of muscle tone triggered by emotion such as laughter, is highly specific and defines narcolepsy type 1
The disorder reflects intrusion of REM-sleep phenomena into wakefulness, explaining cataplexy, dream-like hallucinations, and sleep paralysis
Narcolepsy type 1 is associated with low or undetectable cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin (orexin) and a strong link to the HLA-DQB1*06:02 allele
Diagnosis is supported by overnight polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test showing short sleep latency and multiple sleep-onset REM periods
Management combines scheduled naps and sleep hygiene with wake-promoting agents for sleepiness and specific therapy for cataplexy
Onset is typically in adolescence or young adulthood and the condition is frequently under-recognised for years
Secondary narcolepsy can follow hypothalamic lesions, so consider imaging when there are atypical features or focal signs
reference.pathophysiology: Narcolepsy type 1 results from selective loss of hypocretin (orexin)-producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus, most likely through an autoimmune process in genetically susceptible individuals carrying HLA-DQB1*06:02. Hypocretin normally stabilises wakefulness and suppresses inappropriate REM sleep; its deficiency destabilises the sleep-wake switch, producing daytime sleepiness and the intrusion of REM features such as cataplexy into wakefulness. Type 2 has preserved hypocretin levels and a less well-defined mechanism.
additionalDifferentials: Obstructive sleep apnoea and other causes of fragmented sleep
Syncope or seizures mistaken for cataplexy
additionalInvestigations: Overnight polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test
HLA typing for DQB1*06:02 as a supportive marker
Cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin (orexin) measurement in selected cases
MRI of the brain when secondary narcolepsy from a hypothalamic lesion is suspected
Sleep diaries and actigraphy to exclude insufficient sleep and circadian disorders
redFlags: New hypersomnolence with focal neurological signs or endocrine disturbance suggesting a hypothalamic mass
Severe sleep attacks endangering driving or operating machinery
Status cataplecticus with prolonged, near-continuous cataplexy
Abrupt withdrawal of anticataplectic therapy precipitating rebound cataplexy
reference.prognosis: Narcolepsy is a lifelong disorder, but symptoms can usually be controlled well enough with treatment and behavioural measures to allow good function. It carries important safety implications for driving and work, and untreated disease significantly impairs quality of life, mood, and daytime performance.
pitfalls: Attributing chronic sleepiness to lifestyle or depression and delaying diagnosis for years
Missing cataplexy because patients do not volunteer it or it is mistaken for syncope or seizures
Failing to screen for and address driving and occupational safety risks
Overlooking a secondary hypothalamic cause in atypical or late-onset presentations
management: Combine behavioural measures as first-line treatment of sleepiness, with scheduled daytime naps, a regular sleep schedule and good sleep hygiene
Treat excessive daytime sleepiness with wake-promoting agents such as modafinil, armodafinil, solriamfetol or pitolisant, or with stimulants such as methylphenidate or amfetamines
Treat cataplexy and other REM-intrusion symptoms with sodium oxybate, pitolisant or antidepressants with anticataplectic effect such as SNRIs, SSRIs or tricyclics
Counsel on driving and occupational safety and manage the hazard of untreated sleep attacks
Screen for and manage comorbid mood disorder and disrupted nocturnal sleep
Confirm the diagnosis and subtype with overnight polysomnography and multiple sleep latency testing, referring to a sleep-medicine specialist
Provide long-term follow-up with treatment titration and patient support
